claim: Earnings inequality among Patreon creators within the same content topic doubled between 2015 and 2020, with the Gini coefficient rising from 0.30 to 0.60.
stance_target: Creator income concentration worsened as the creator economy matured
scope_conditions: Complete Patreon transaction record June 2013 to December 2020, over USD 2 billion in pledges; measures Patreon subscription income only, not total creator income; Patreon's creator base is heavily US/Western
quoted_support: The Gini coefficient across creators within a topic has steadily and substantially increased from 0.30 in 2015 to 0.60 in December 2020
region: Global platform, US/Western-skewed creator base; no country breakdown reported

claim: Concentration within topics rose while concentration across topics fell, so the platform's apparent diversification masks worsening inequality among the creators actually competing with each other.
stance_target: Aggregate platform diversity statistics conceal creator-level inequality
scope_conditions: Patreon 2013-2020; the across-topic decline begins mid-2015 after an initial concentration phase when most creators came from YouTube
quoted_support: ever since mid-2015, there has been a steady, minor decrease in the platform topic Gini coefficient from 0.80 to 0.72, indicating that aggregate pledging on Patreon has supported a slightly more diverse set of topics over time. However, although the earnings distribution has become slightly more distributed across topics, it has become significantly more concentrated within topics over time.

claim: Top-decile Patreon creators receive nearly $15 per pledge while bottom-decile creators receive $2, so high earners win on price per supporter as well as on audience size, compounding the gap multiplicatively.
stance_target: Creator earnings gaps are multiplicative, not merely proportional to audience
scope_conditions: Creators grouped into deciles by total earnings on Patreon 2013-2020; pledge amounts only, not total creator income
quoted_support: The highest-earning creators receive almost $15 per pledge, whereas the lowest earners receive only $2 per pledge. Thus not only do high-earning creators attract larger audiences, they also attract far larger pledges per patron.
numbers: >$12 spread across modalities at the top

claim: Audiences of the largest Patreon creators pledge to another creator only 40% of the time, versus 90% for the smallest creators, meaning top creators pull in one-and-done supporters who do not circulate to other creators.
stance_target: Success at the top does not spill over to smaller creators
scope_conditions: Multi-patronage measured as the fraction of a creator's patrons who pledge to at least one other creator, at a given time; Patreon has no recommendation algorithm and no patron social network, so this is organic behaviour
quoted_support: the audiences of the largest creators pledge to other creators 40% of the time, while the audiences of the smallest creators are multi-patrons 90% of the time —over a 50 percentage point difference between the largest and smallest creators. This reveals that large creators often inspire “one-and-done” patrons

claim: Patrons who support only one creator churn off the platform more often than patrons who spread pledges across many creators, so the most emotionally committed supporters are the least durable revenue source.
stance_target: Fan-funded creator income is structurally unstable at small scale
scope_conditions: Patreon patron-level transaction data 2013-2020; churn defined as having no active pledge at t+k; effect on loyalty is larger than the effect on churn
quoted_support: Patrons who pledge to a narrow set of creators are more loyal, but churn off the platform more often.
numbers: churn gap between highest and lowest activity levels: 1-2 percentage points
uni-patrons retained 6 percentage points less than average

claim: Patreon operates with no recommendation algorithm and no patron social network, with patrons arriving only via search or off-platform links, which makes it a rare algorithm-free control case for isolating recommendation-system effects on creator earnings.
stance_target: Methodological framing for separating algorithmic from non-algorithmic drivers of creator income inequality
scope_conditions: Describes Patreon as of the 2013-2020 study window
quoted_support: Activity on Patreon is particularly organic, as the platform does not offer algorithmic or human-curated recommendations, and there is no notion of a patron-patron social network. As such, patrons can only arrive at a creator's page via search or via an off-platform link.

claim: Smaller Patreon creators show higher relative audience growth than large ones and every earnings decile grew in absolute terms from 2013 to 2020, which cuts against a pure winner-take-all reading of the platform.
stance_target: Creator markets are strictly winner-take-all with no room for new entrants
scope_conditions: Deciles are pinned to the December 2013 earnings bands and creators are reclassified into them over time, so 'decile growth' partly reflects platform-wide expansion; relative growth from a small base is easier; does not contradict the rising within-topic Gini
quoted_support: Interestingly, smaller creators exhibit higher relative growth in audience size, revealing that it is also possible for newcomers on the platform to gain prominence.

claim: Patreon paid over USD 2 billion to creators between 2013 and 2020 and over USD 100 million per month at the end of that period, establishing the absolute scale of the fan-funding channel.
stance_target: Establishing the size of direct fan funding relative to other creator revenue
scope_conditions: Platform-reported totals, gross of Patreon's own fee
quoted_support: than $100M to creators every month and has directed more than $2B in revenue to creators since its inception in 2013.
